articles.title: Why Does My Cat Meow at Night? 8 Causes and How to Stop It
articles.metaDescription: Is your cat keeping you awake? Learn 8 reasons for nighttime meowing, a 7-day reset plan, and when yowling signals a medical emergency that needs a vet.
articles.alt: Alert cat sitting in a quiet living room at night
articles.summary: Learn why cats meow at night, how to identify common triggers, what changes can improve nighttime routines, and when persistent vocalization needs veterinary attention.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat meow at night
secondaryKeywords: how to stop cat meowing at night
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Quick Answer

Cats may meow at night because of hunger, boredom, attention-seeking, environmental triggers, stress, age-related changes, pain, or illness. A young healthy cat that is active and otherwise normal may improve with a better daytime routine, but sudden or intense nighttime vocalization—especially in an older cat—deserves veterinary attention.

Why Cats Become More Vocal at Night

Cats are naturally most active around dawn and dusk, and many indoor cats sleep for long periods during the day. If a cat has unused energy, a quiet house at night can become the perfect time to explore, play, ask for food, or seek attention. Some cats also learn that meowing brings a response, so the behavior becomes stronger over time.

1. Hunger or a Feeding Schedule That Ends Too Early

If dinner is several hours before bedtime, a cat may wake hungry during the night. Splitting the daily food allowance into several smaller meals can help. For some households, a timed feeder that delivers a small overnight portion is useful. Keep the total daily calories appropriate so that solving nighttime meowing does not create weight gain.

2. Boredom and Excess Energy

Short play sessions during the day and a more active session in the evening can reduce nighttime activity. Use toys that encourage stalking, chasing, and pouncing, then allow the cat to settle. Rotate toys rather than leaving every toy available all the time.

3. Attention-Seeking

If the cat is healthy and its needs are met, repeated talking, petting, or feeding after every nighttime meow can unintentionally reward the behavior. Consistency matters. Do not punish or frighten the cat; instead, increase positive interaction earlier in the day and avoid reinforcing unnecessary nighttime demands.

4. Stress or Environmental Change

Moving, a new pet, visitors, construction noise, outdoor cats near windows, or changes in routine can increase vocalization. Provide predictable feeding and play times, safe hiding places, vertical resting spaces, and quiet sleeping areas. Blocking a stressful nighttime view through a window can also help in some cases.

5. Mating-Related Vocalization

Unspayed females may yowl when in heat, and intact males may become restless or vocal when they detect a female nearby. Neutering or spaying usually reduces mating-related behavior and also provides important health and population-control benefits.

6. Pain or Medical Illness

Pain, urinary disease, high blood pressure, thyroid disease, kidney disease, gastrointestinal discomfort, and other medical problems can change a cat's behavior. Sudden new vocalization is more concerning than a lifelong habit. Watch for weight change, thirst, urination changes, vomiting, hiding, restlessness, or reduced mobility.

7. Age-Related Cognitive or Sensory Changes

Senior cats may vocalize because of reduced vision or hearing, disorientation, or cognitive decline. Night lights, familiar pathways, easily accessible food and water, and a predictable routine can help. A veterinarian should first rule out medical causes because many illnesses can mimic cognitive decline.

A Practical 7-Day Reset

For a healthy cat, keep wake time and meal times consistent, add two or three short daytime play sessions, schedule the most active play session before the final meal, provide enrichment, and avoid rewarding unnecessary nighttime calls. Track whether the pattern improves over one week.

When to Call the Vet

Arrange veterinary care if nighttime meowing is sudden, persistent, worsening, or associated with weight loss, increased thirst, changes in urination, vomiting, weakness, breathing changes, apparent pain, confusion, or major behavior change. Older cats with new nighttime yowling deserve particular attention.

Bottom Line

Nighttime meowing is often a mix of routine, energy, feeding, and learned behavior, but medical causes must not be overlooked. Improve the daytime schedule first only when the cat is otherwise well, and seek veterinary evaluation for sudden or unexplained changes.

articles.title: How to Get Your Cat to Drink More Water: 12 Vet-Approved Tips
articles.metaDescription: Is your cat not drinking enough? Discover 12 safe hydration tips, from fountains to wet food, plus 5 warning signs that increased thirst needs a vet visit.
articles.alt: Cat drinking fresh water from a wide clean bowl
articles.summary: Learn how to get your cat to drink more water with 12 safe hydration tips, plus bowl, fountain, wet food and veterinary warning-sign guidance.
articles.primaryKeyword: how to get your cat to drink more water
secondaryKeywords: how much water should a cat drink
how to get my cat to drink water
how to make cats drink more water
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Quick Answer

To encourage a cat to drink more, offer fresh water in several quiet locations, use wide clean bowls, experiment with ceramic, glass, or stainless steel, consider a fountain, and increase moisture through wet food when appropriate. A sudden increase in thirst is different from simply wanting to improve hydration and should be discussed with a veterinarian.

Why Cats May Drink Less Than Owners Expect

Cats evolved from ancestors adapted to relatively dry environments and often obtain a meaningful portion of water from food. A cat eating wet food may visit the water bowl less often than a cat eating dry food. The goal is not to force a specific number of bowl visits, but to support adequate overall hydration.

1. Put Water in More Than One Place

Some cats avoid a single bowl because it is near a noisy appliance, busy walkway, litter box, or another pet. Place water in several calm areas of the home so the cat has options.

2. Use a Wide, Shallow Bowl

Many cats prefer bowls that do not press against the whiskers. A wide, shallow bowl can be more comfortable and allows the cat to see the surrounding area while drinking.

3. Keep Water Fresh

Wash bowls daily and replace water regularly. Biofilm and odors can make a bowl less appealing even when it looks clean. Avoid strong detergents or fragrances that leave a smell behind.

4. Try Different Bowl Materials

Some cats prefer ceramic, glass, or stainless steel over plastic. Plastic can scratch and retain odors. Test one variable at a time so you can tell what the cat actually prefers.

5. Consider a Cat Fountain

Moving water attracts some cats. If you use a fountain, clean it thoroughly and replace filters according to the manufacturer's instructions. A dirty fountain can become less appealing than a simple bowl.

6. Separate Water From Food

Some cats drink more when water is placed away from the food bowl. Try a few locations and observe which one the cat chooses most often.

7. Add Moisture Through Food

Wet food naturally contains more water than dry food. If your cat can eat wet food safely, replacing part of the diet or adding a small amount of water to wet food can increase total fluid intake. Make diet changes gradually and follow veterinary advice for cats on prescription diets.

8. Offer Multiple Temperatures

Some cats prefer cool water, while others seem to like room-temperature water. Small preferences can influence how often a cat drinks.

9. Use Water-Rich Treats Carefully

Veterinary-approved broth products made specifically for cats can sometimes increase fluid intake. Avoid broths containing onion, garlic, excessive salt, or other ingredients that are unsafe for cats.

10. Make Drinking Easy for Senior Cats

Older cats with arthritis may avoid bowls that require stairs, jumping, or awkward neck positions. Keep water on the same level where the cat spends most of its time and use stable, easy-to-reach bowls.

11. Monitor the Litter Box

Urine output gives useful context. Very small urine clumps, straining, frequent trips, or inability to urinate are not problems to solve by simply adding more water. Male cats that cannot urinate need emergency veterinary care.

12. Watch for Increased Thirst

Drinking more than usual can occur with kidney disease, diabetes, thyroid disease, some medications, and other conditions. If you notice a persistent increase in both drinking and urination, schedule a veterinary examination rather than assuming the change is healthy.

Bottom Line

Make water easy, clean, and appealing, and use wet food strategically when appropriate. The best hydration plan is one your individual cat willingly uses. Sudden or marked changes in thirst should be treated as a health clue, not merely a hydration preference.

articles.title: Why Is My Cat Not Eating? 7 Critical Causes and When to Rush to the Vet
articles.metaDescription: Is your cat not eating? Learn common causes, safe home checks, why prolonged appetite loss matters, and when veterinary care is urgent.
articles.alt: Cat sitting beside a food bowl while an owner monitors its appetite
articles.summary: Understand why a cat may stop eating, what you can safely check at home, why prolonged appetite loss matters, and when a veterinarian should evaluate the problem.
articles.primaryKeyword: why is my cat not eating
secondaryKeywords: when to call vet cat not eating
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Quick Answer

A cat that stops eating should be taken seriously, especially if the change is sudden or lasts into the next day. Causes range from stress and dental pain to gastrointestinal disease, infection, kidney disease, pancreatitis, medication effects, and other illnesses. Cats can develop complications when they eat too little for too long, so persistent appetite loss needs veterinary assessment.

Why Appetite Loss Matters in Cats

Cats are not small dogs when it comes to fasting. Prolonged inadequate food intake can contribute to hepatic lipidosis, particularly in overweight cats. The risk varies with the individual cat and the underlying disease, so waiting several days for appetite to return can be unsafe.

1. Dental or Mouth Pain

Dental disease, tooth resorption, gingivitis, stomatitis, oral ulcers, and jaw pain can make eating uncomfortable. A cat may approach food, sniff it, then walk away, chew on one side, drop food, drool, or prefer soft food.

2. Nausea and Gastrointestinal Disease

Nausea can occur with stomach or intestinal disease, pancreatitis, dietary problems, toxins, and many systemic illnesses. Lip licking, repeated swallowing, drooling, hiding, or turning away after smelling food can accompany nausea.

3. Stress and Environmental Change

Moving, boarding, a new pet, construction, visitors, or conflict around the feeding area can temporarily reduce appetite. Still, stress should be a diagnosis of exclusion when appetite loss is significant or persistent.

4. Respiratory Disease

Cats rely heavily on smell when deciding to eat. Nasal congestion can reduce food interest. Warmed wet food may smell stronger, but breathing difficulty, severe congestion, fever, or lethargy requires veterinary care.

5. Kidney, Liver, or Endocrine Disease

Systemic illnesses can suppress appetite through nausea, dehydration, pain, or metabolic changes. Weight loss, increased thirst, vomiting, weakness, or changes in urination provide important clues.

6. Pain Anywhere in the Body

Arthritis, abdominal pain, injury, urinary discomfort, and other painful conditions can reduce appetite. Cats often hide pain, so behavior changes may be subtle.

7. Medication or Toxin Exposure

Some medications can cause nausea or appetite changes, while toxins can cause sudden refusal to eat along with vomiting, weakness, tremors, or drooling. Bring product packaging to the veterinarian if exposure is possible.

Safe Things to Check at Home

Confirm that the cat can access food, that the food is fresh, and that another pet is not blocking the bowl. Offer a familiar, palatable food in a quiet location. Do not force-feed a nauseated or weak cat unless a veterinarian has instructed you, because aspiration and food aversion are possible.

When Veterinary Care Is Urgent

Seek prompt veterinary care if a cat refuses all food, especially when the problem approaches 24 hours, or sooner if the cat is a kitten, diabetic, elderly, overweight, or already ill. Emergency care is appropriate for appetite loss with repeated vomiting, severe weakness, collapse, breathing difficulty, suspected poisoning, a swollen painful abdomen, or inability to urinate.

What the Vet May Do

The veterinarian may examine the mouth, assess hydration and pain, and recommend bloodwork, urinalysis, imaging, or other tests based on the history. Treatment may include fluids, anti-nausea medication, pain control, appetite support, and treatment of the underlying cause.

Bottom Line

A missed meal is not always an emergency, but persistent appetite loss in cats should never be ignored. The safest approach is to identify the cause early rather than trying increasingly tempting foods for several days.

articles.title: Why Does My Cat Bite Me? 5 Triggers and How to Stop It Safely
articles.metaDescription: Learn why cats may bite during play, petting, fear, frustration, or pain, how to read warning signs, and how to reduce biting without punishment.
articles.alt: Cat interacting calmly with an owner who is watching its body language
articles.summary: Learn why cats bite during petting, play, fear, frustration or pain, how to read warning signals, reduce triggers, and know when sudden aggression needs professional help.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat bite me
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Quick Answer

Cats bite for many reasons, including play, overstimulation, fear, frustration, redirected arousal, and pain. The solution depends on what happens immediately before the bite. Punishment usually increases fear and can make biting worse.

1. Play Biting

Kittens and young cats learn hunting skills through stalking, grabbing, and biting. Hands and feet should not become toys. Redirect play to wand toys, kicker toys, and other objects that create distance between teeth and skin.

2. Petting Overstimulation

Some cats enjoy petting only for a limited time. Early warning signs can include tail flicking, skin twitching, ears turning sideways, pupils enlarging, or the cat looking sharply toward your hand. Stop before the cat feels the need to bite.

3. Fear and Defensive Biting

A frightened cat may bite when cornered, restrained, picked up, or approached by a stranger. Give the cat space and an escape route. Forcing contact can intensify defensive behavior.

4. Pain-Related Biting

A cat that suddenly starts biting when touched may be painful. Dental disease, arthritis, wounds, ear disease, abdominal pain, and many other problems can reduce tolerance for handling. Sudden aggression deserves a veterinary examination.

5. Redirected Aggression

A cat that becomes highly aroused by an outdoor cat, loud noise, or conflict may bite a nearby person even though that person was not the original trigger. Do not grab or restrain an intensely aroused cat. Give it time and space to calm down.

How to Reduce Biting Safely

Identify patterns, stop using hands as toys, provide daily interactive play, respect body-language warnings, and reward calm interaction. If biting occurs during petting, shorten sessions and focus on areas the cat consistently enjoys.

What Not to Do

Do not hit, yell at, spray, or physically punish the cat. Punishment can increase fear and may suppress warning signals without changing the underlying emotion, making future bites harder to predict.

If a Bite Breaks the Skin

Cat bites can introduce bacteria deep into tissue. Wash the area promptly with soap and water and seek medical advice for puncture wounds, swelling, redness, worsening pain, fever, or bites to the hand, face, or joints.

When to Seek Veterinary or Behavior Help

Arrange veterinary evaluation for sudden new aggression, pain signs, neurologic changes, or a major change in personality. A qualified feline behavior professional can help when medical causes have been addressed but biting remains frequent or dangerous.

Bottom Line

Biting is communication. The fastest route to improvement is identifying the trigger, preventing rehearsal of the behavior, and teaching safer alternatives rather than punishing the cat.

articles.title: Bringing a New Cat Home? A Calm First-Week Setup That Works
articles.metaDescription: New cat hiding? Follow this step-by-step first-week guide: safe room setup, resident cat introduction, and signs your cat is ready to explore the whole home.
articles.alt: New cat exploring a quiet prepared room with bed water and toys
articles.summary: Prepare a safe room, help a newly adopted cat settle during the first days, expand access gradually, and recognize signs that stress or illness needs attention.
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Quick Answer

The calmest way to bring a new cat home is to start with one quiet safe room containing food, water, litter, hiding places, a bed, scratching options, and toys. Let the cat settle before giving access to the entire home, and introduce resident pets gradually.

Prepare the Safe Room Before Arrival

Choose a low-traffic room with a door that closes securely. Place food and water away from the litter box. Add at least one covered hiding place and one elevated resting option if possible. Remove hazards such as toxic plants, strings, open windows, and small objects that can be swallowed.

Day 1: Keep the Environment Small

Open the carrier in the safe room and allow the cat to come out voluntarily. Do not pull a frightened cat from the carrier. Sit quietly nearby, speak softly, and allow hiding. Some cats explore immediately while others need hours or days.

Days 2–3: Build Predictability

Feed on a consistent schedule, clean the litter box regularly, and use short calm visits. Interactive play can help confident cats, but do not force play or handling. Watch appetite, urination, defecation, and general behavior.

Days 3–5: Expand Gradually

When the cat is eating normally, using the litter box, grooming, and approaching people comfortably, allow brief exploration of one additional area while the rest of the home remains controlled.

If You Have Another Cat

Keep the cats physically separated at first. Exchange bedding or soft cloths carrying each cat's scent. Feed on opposite sides of a closed door, then progress to visual contact through a safe barrier only when both cats remain calm.

If You Have a Dog

Use a leash and barrier for early meetings. The cat should always have an escape route and access to elevated spaces. Reward the dog for calm behavior and never allow chasing.

Signs the Cat Is Ready for More Space

Good signs include regular eating, normal litter-box use, relaxed grooming, play, sleeping in open areas, and curious exploration. Hiding alone is not always a problem, but persistent refusal to eat or worsening fear requires attention.

Common Mistakes

Avoid introducing the new cat to every room and pet immediately, forcing handling, changing food suddenly, placing the litter box near noisy appliances, or allowing children and visitors to overwhelm the cat.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Seek veterinary advice if the new cat refuses food, repeatedly vomits, has diarrhea, strains to urinate, has breathing difficulty, appears extremely lethargic, or shows signs of pain. Newly adopted cats should also receive routine veterinary care appropriate to their history.

Bottom Line

A successful first week is usually quiet, predictable, and gradual. Confidence grows faster when the cat controls the pace instead of being pushed into the full household immediately.

articles.title: How to Introduce Two Cats: A 5-Stage Guide That Prevents Fights
articles.metaDescription: Stop cat fights before they start. Follow this 5-stage introduction plan: scent swapping, barrier meetings, supervised contact, and signs to slow down.
articles.alt: Two cats calmly observing each other from a comfortable distance indoors
articles.summary: A practical resident-cat introduction plan using separation, scent exchange, barrier meetings and short supervised contact to reduce fear and conflict.
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Quick Answer

Successful cat introductions are usually gradual. Start with complete separation, exchange scents, create positive associations near a closed door, progress to visual meetings through a barrier, and only then allow short supervised contact.

Stage 1: Complete Separation

Give the new cat a dedicated room with its own food, water, litter box, resting places, and scratching surface. The resident cat should keep access to familiar resources. This reduces territorial pressure and prevents immediate conflict.

Stage 2: Scent Exchange

Swap bedding, blankets, or toys between the cats. You can also gently rub a clean cloth on the cheek area of one cat and place it near the other cat's resting space. Do not force the scent directly onto either cat.

Stage 3: Positive Associations at the Door

Feed high-value meals or treats on opposite sides of the closed door, starting far enough away that both cats remain relaxed. Over several sessions, move bowls gradually closer only if neither cat shows escalating stress.

Stage 4: Visual Contact Through a Barrier

Use a secure screen, baby gate setup, or slightly opened door that prevents physical contact. Keep sessions short. Reward calm looking, sniffing, or disengaging. End the session before staring, growling, swatting, or chasing escalates.

Stage 5: Short Supervised Meetings

Allow brief contact in a room with multiple escape routes and elevated spaces. Use toys or treats to keep the environment positive. Do not hold the cats nose-to-nose or force proximity.

How Fast Should You Progress?

There is no universal timeline. Some cats progress in days while others need several weeks or longer. The correct pace is determined by behavior, not the calendar.

Normal Tension vs. a Serious Fight

Brief hissing or a single swat can occur during adjustment. Repeated chasing, cornering, screaming, biting, fur flying, or injuries indicate the process is moving too quickly and the cats should be separated again.

Resource Setup Matters

Provide multiple litter boxes, resting places, food and water stations, scratching options, and vertical spaces. Competition for resources can maintain conflict even after the initial introduction seems successful.

Do Not Punish Either Cat

Punishment can make each cat associate the other with fear. Instead, increase distance, return to an easier stage, and reward calm behavior.

When to Get Professional Help

Seek veterinary or behavior support if aggression causes injuries, one cat stops eating or using the litter box, fear remains intense, or repeated careful introductions fail. Pain and medical illness can also worsen inter-cat aggression.

Bottom Line

Slow introductions are faster than repairing a bad first meeting. Build tolerance in small steps and let calm behavior—not impatience—decide when to advance.

articles.title: Why Does My Cat Follow Me Everywhere? 7 Reasons and When to Worry
articles.metaDescription: Is your cat clingy? Learn 7 reasons cats follow owners (love, routine, boredom, anxiety) and when sudden clinginess signals a health problem needing a vet.
articles.alt: Cat calmly following its owner through a bright home hallway
articles.summary: Discover why cats follow their owners from room to room, how attention, routine, curiosity and stress can contribute, and when clingy behavior may signal a health problem.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat follow me everywhere
secondaryKeywords: why does my cat follow me room to room
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Quick Answer

Cats may follow their owners because of attachment, curiosity, routine, food expectations, boredom, social preference, or stress. A lifelong habit is usually normal, but sudden clinginess can sometimes accompany pain, illness, sensory decline, or anxiety.

1. Your Cat Enjoys Your Company

Many cats form strong social bonds with people. Following from room to room can simply be a way to stay near a preferred companion.

2. Routine Predicts Rewards

Cats learn household patterns quickly. Walking toward the kitchen may predict food, while entering the bedroom may predict attention or play. Following can therefore become part of a daily routine.

3. Curiosity

Closed doors, moving objects, running water, and human activity are interesting. A cat may follow because each room offers new smells, sounds, or opportunities to investigate.

4. Boredom

Indoor cats with limited stimulation may use their owner as the main source of entertainment. Add climbing spaces, scratching surfaces, puzzle feeders, window views, and daily interactive play.

5. Attention-Seeking

If following reliably leads to petting, treats, or conversation, the behavior is reinforced. That is not necessarily a problem unless the cat becomes distressed when attention is unavailable.

6. Stress or Insecurity

A new home, schedule change, new animal, visitor, or outdoor threat can make a cat stay closer to a trusted person. Provide predictable routines and safe resting areas where the cat can withdraw voluntarily.

7. Medical or Age-Related Change

Senior cats with reduced vision, hearing loss, cognitive changes, or medical illness may seek more proximity. Pain or systemic disease can also alter social behavior. Sudden clinginess should be evaluated in context with appetite, weight, thirst, mobility, and litter-box changes.

When Following Is Healthy

It is usually harmless when the cat can relax alone, eats and sleeps normally, plays, uses the litter box normally, and does not panic when separated briefly.

When to Be Concerned

Contact a veterinarian if following behavior changes suddenly or appears with vocalization, confusion, weight loss, increased thirst, weakness, hiding, reduced appetite, or other new symptoms.

How to Encourage Healthy Independence

Reward the cat for using beds, perches, and enrichment away from you. Avoid abruptly pushing the cat away; instead, create attractive alternatives and maintain regular social time.

Bottom Line

Following is often a sign of social interest and routine. The important question is whether it is normal for your cat or represents a sudden behavior change accompanied by other signs.

articles.title: How to Trim a Cat's Nails Safely: Step-by-Step (Without the Stress)
articles.metaDescription: Fear-free nail trimming! Learn how to handle paws, identify the quick, use sharp clippers, and what to do if you cut too short. Plus when to call the vet.
articles.alt: Owner gently holding a relaxed cat paw during a safe nail trim
articles.summary: Learn how to trim cat nails safely, introduce paw handling gradually, identify the quick, avoid common mistakes, and know when a groomer or veterinarian should help.
articles.primaryKeyword: how to trim cat nails safely
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Quick Answer

Trim cat nails by using sharp cat nail clippers, handling one paw at a time, pressing gently to extend the claw, and cutting only the clear hooked tip. Avoid the pink quick. Short, calm sessions are safer than trying to finish every nail at once.

What You Need

Use cat-specific nail clippers or small scissor-style pet clippers, good lighting, treats, and optional styptic powder in case a nail is accidentally cut too short. Do not use dull tools that crush the nail.

Step 1: Teach Paw Handling First

Before trimming, touch the shoulder, leg, and paw briefly while the cat is relaxed. Reward calm behavior. Over several sessions, progress to gently pressing a toe pad so the claw extends.

Step 2: Identify the Quick

In light-colored claws, the quick is the pink area containing blood vessels and nerves. The safe cutting zone is the sharp transparent tip beyond it. With dark claws, remove only a small amount at a time.

Step 3: Position the Cat Comfortably

Choose a quiet location and a position the cat already tolerates. Some cats are comfortable on a lap, while others do better standing on a nonslip surface. Avoid scruffing or forceful restraint.

Step 4: Clip the Hooked Tip

Extend one claw and make a quick clean cut through the narrow tip. Do not trim close to the quick merely to make the nail shorter. Conservative trimming is safer.

Step 5: Stop Before the Cat Becomes Frustrated

One or two paws per session is perfectly acceptable. Ending while the cat is still calm helps future trims become easier.

If You Cut the Quick

Apply gentle pressure with gauze and use styptic powder if available. Minor bleeding often stops quickly, but persistent bleeding, severe pain, or a torn nail requires veterinary attention.

How Often Do Cats Need Nail Trims?

Many indoor cats need trimming every few weeks, but growth rates vary. Check nails regularly rather than following a rigid schedule. Senior cats may need more frequent checks because they may scratch less and develop overgrown claws.

Do Scratching Posts Replace Nail Trimming?

Scratching helps remove outer claw layers and supports normal behavior, but it does not always keep nails short enough. Both scratching surfaces and periodic nail checks are useful.

When a Professional Should Help

Ask a veterinarian or groomer for help if the cat becomes extremely fearful, if nails are embedded in paw pads, if a claw is split or infected, or if handling causes pain.

Bottom Line

Safe trimming is about removing only the sharp tip and keeping the experience low stress. Slow training and conservative cuts are more important than finishing every nail in one session.

articles.title: Why Is My Cat Sneezing? 6 Causes and When It's a Vet Emergency
articles.metaDescription: Occasional sneeze or something more? Learn common causes of cat sneezing, what accompanying signs matter, and when breathing problems need urgent veterinary care.
articles.alt: Cat resting comfortably while its owner watches for sneezing and nasal symptoms
articles.summary: Learn what can cause cat sneezing, which accompanying symptoms matter, what you can safely monitor at home, and when respiratory signs require veterinary attention.
secondaryKeywords: when to call vet for cat sneezing
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Quick Answer

An occasional sneeze can be harmless, but repeated sneezing may result from upper respiratory infection, nasal irritation, dental disease, foreign material, inflammation, or less commonly other nasal disorders. Breathing difficulty, open-mouth breathing, marked lethargy, or refusal to eat requires prompt veterinary attention.

1. Upper Respiratory Infection

Viral and bacterial infections are common causes of sneezing, especially in kittens, newly adopted cats, shelter cats, or cats living in multi-cat environments. Signs may include eye discharge, nasal discharge, congestion, fever, and reduced appetite.

2. Irritants in the Environment

Dusty litter, smoke, aerosols, perfume, cleaning sprays, and renovation dust can irritate the nose. Remove obvious irritants and improve ventilation, but persistent sneezing should not automatically be blamed on the environment.

3. Dental Disease

Upper tooth-root disease can sometimes affect structures near the nasal cavity. Bad breath, difficulty chewing, drooling, facial swelling, or one-sided nasal discharge increases concern for oral or dental disease.

4. Foreign Material

Plant material, dust, or other small particles can enter the nasal passages. Sudden intense sneezing, pawing at the nose, or one-sided discharge may occur. Do not insert tweezers or other objects into the nostril.

5. Chronic Nasal Inflammation

Some cats develop persistent rhinitis after earlier respiratory disease or from ongoing inflammation. These cats may have recurrent congestion or discharge and require veterinary evaluation to rule out other causes.

6. Polyps, Masses, or Other Structural Problems

Persistent one-sided discharge, blood from the nose, facial asymmetry, noisy breathing, or symptoms that do not respond as expected may require imaging or more advanced examination.

What Nasal Discharge Can Tell You

Clear discharge can occur with mild irritation or early respiratory disease, while thicker yellow or green discharge can accompany inflammation or infection. Blood, foul odor, or persistent one-sided discharge warrants veterinary assessment.

Safe Home Support

Keep the cat warm and comfortable, gently wipe nasal discharge with a soft damp cloth, and offer palatable food. Humidified air may help some congested cats. Do not give human cold medicines, decongestants, or essential oils.

When It Is Urgent

Seek urgent care for open-mouth breathing, severe respiratory effort, blue or very pale gums, collapse, severe weakness, or inability to eat or drink because of breathing difficulty.

When to Schedule a Vet Visit

Arrange veterinary care when sneezing is frequent, lasts more than a few days, is accompanied by eye or nasal discharge, appetite loss, fever, weight loss, facial swelling, or recurrent episodes.

Bottom Line

One sneeze is usually not a crisis, but repeated sneezing is a symptom worth interpreting with the cat's breathing, appetite, discharge, energy level, and duration of illness.

articles.title: Why Is My Cat Always Hungry? 5 Causes and When to See a Vet
articles.metaDescription: Is your cat begging constantly? Learn 5 reasons for increased appetite (boredom, diabetes, hyperthyroidism), track weight, and when hunger + weight loss is dangerous.
articles.alt: Cat waiting beside a measured food portion while its owner checks feeding routine
articles.summary: Learn why a cat may seem hungry all the time, how feeding habits and boredom can contribute, what health changes matter, and when increased appetite needs veterinary evaluation.
articles.primaryKeyword: why is my cat always hungry
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Quick Answer

A cat that always seems hungry may simply be underfed, highly food-motivated, bored, or eating a diet that does not provide enough satiety. However, increased appetite can also occur with hyperthyroidism, diabetes, intestinal disease, parasites, or other medical problems—especially when hunger is accompanied by weight loss.

1. The Daily Portion May Be Too Small

Feeding recommendations on packaging are only starting points. Calorie needs vary with age, body size, activity, reproductive status, and health. A veterinarian can help determine an appropriate daily calorie target.

2. Feeding Pattern Can Affect Satiety

Some cats do better with several smaller meals rather than one or two large meals. Puzzle feeders and slow feeders can extend mealtime and provide mental stimulation.

3. Boredom Can Look Like Hunger

A cat may ask for food because eating is the most predictable activity in the day. Increase interactive play, climbing, scratching, window enrichment, and food puzzles before assuming every request means true hunger.

4. Hyperthyroidism

Hyperthyroidism is common in older cats and can cause increased appetite together with weight loss, restlessness, vomiting, diarrhea, increased thirst, or a faster heart rate. Blood testing is used to evaluate thyroid function.

5. Diabetes Mellitus

Some diabetic cats eat more while losing weight because their bodies cannot use glucose normally. Increased thirst and urination are common accompanying signs.

6. Intestinal Disease or Poor Nutrient Absorption

Chronic intestinal disease can interfere with digestion or nutrient absorption. Weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, or poor coat quality may occur even when appetite remains strong.

7. Parasites

Intestinal parasites can contribute to weight loss or poor condition in some cats, particularly kittens and outdoor cats. Diagnosis and treatment should be based on veterinary guidance rather than routine deworming with random products.

Track Weight, Not Appetite Alone

A cat that begs frequently but maintains an ideal stable weight is different from a cat that eats eagerly while steadily losing weight. Monthly weight checks can reveal trends that are difficult to notice by appearance alone.

Avoid Solving Begging With Unlimited Food

Free feeding can lead to obesity in some cats. Excess body weight increases the risk of diabetes, arthritis, and other health problems. Use measured portions and adjust based on body condition and veterinary advice.

When to See a Veterinarian

Schedule an examination if increased appetite is new, persistent, or accompanied by weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, increased thirst, increased urination, weakness, or behavior change. Older cats with new excessive hunger should be evaluated rather than simply fed more.

Bottom Line

Constant hunger can be behavioral, nutritional, or medical. The key distinction is whether the cat's weight, thirst, urination, stool, energy, or overall health is changing at the same time.
